script.title: Why He Scratched Cow Pus Into a Boy

lines: A doctor scratched cow pus into a healthy boy's arm.
It was England, 1796.
In towns, smallpox killed one person in five.
Doctors already had a risky shield.
They rubbed real smallpox into scratches on healthy skin.
Most people got a milder case. Some died.
Edward Jenner knew that risk.
As a boy, he got that treatment, and it hurt his health for life.
Jenner believed cowpox, a mild disease from cows, could protect people.
In May 1796, he scraped pus from the blisters of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes.
She had caught cowpox from a cow called Blossom.
Then Jenner made two small cuts in the arm of James Phipps, his gardener's eight-year-old son.
He rubbed the cowpox pus inside.
James got a fever and felt uneasy. Then he was fine.
You see, it's like a fire drill.
The body practices on a small fire, so it's ready for the real one.
Next, Jenner did the frightening part.
He put real smallpox into the boy.
James did not get sick.
Jenner's Latin name for cowpox gave the world a new word: vaccine.
In 1840, Britain banned the old method and made vaccination free.
And Blossom's hide still hangs on a wall in a London medical school library.

claims.claim: Smallpox killed as many as 20% of people in towns and cities in Jenner's time.
Variolation scratched smallpox material into the skin; it usually caused a milder infection, but some died.
Jenner was inoculated by variolation as a boy, which had a lifelong effect on his health.
On 14 May 1796 Jenner scraped pus from cowpox blisters on the hands of milkmaid Sarah Nelmes, who caught cowpox from a cow called Blossom.
Jenner inoculated James Phipps, his gardener's eight-year-old son, through two small cuts; it caused a fever and some uneasiness.
Jenner later injected Phipps with smallpox material and no disease followed.
The word vaccine comes from Variolae vaccinae, Jenner's term for cowpox.
In 1840 the British government banned variolation and provided cowpox vaccination free of charge.
Blossom's hide hangs on the wall of the St George's Medical School library in London.
